positions/fundamentalism/oneLine: Christians must defend the non-negotiable "fundamentals" of historic faith (an inerrant Bible, the virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, bodily resurrection, miracles and Christ’s return) against modernism, and separate from churches that deny them.
positions/fundamentalism/coreClaims/0: The Bible is verbally inspired and inerrant in its original manuscripts.
positions/fundamentalism/coreClaims/1: The virgin birth, substitutionary atonement, bodily resurrection, miracles and the personal return of Christ are essential.
positions/fundamentalism/coreClaims/2: Modernist theology is apostasy, not an acceptable variant of Christianity.
positions/fundamentalism/coreClaims/3: Faithful Christians must contend for the faith and, where necessary, separate from apostate institutions (ecclesiastical separation).
positions/fundamentalism/coreClaims/4: Usually premillennial, often dispensational, with strong emphasis on evangelism.
positions/fundamentalism/origin: Emerged from 19th-century premillennial Bible conferences (Niagara, 1878), Princeton inerrancy (A. A. Hodge and B. B. Warfield, 1881) and opposition to higher criticism. The Presbyterian General Assembly’s five fundamentals (1910) and The Fundamentals (1910–15) gave it a platform; Curtis Lee Laws coined the name in 1920; William Bell Riley’s World’s Christian Fundamentals Association (1919), the Scopes trial (1925) and the founding of separatist bodies (Orthodox Presbyterian Church, 1936; Bob Jones University) followed. The term is now also applied, often loosely, to conservative movements in other religions.
positions/fundamentalism/strongestArgume: It defended doctrines held by virtually all Christians for nineteen centuries and confessed in the creeds against those who denied them.
Its leaders included serious scholars (Machen, Warfield) whose arguments that liberalism was a different religion were acknowledged even by some secular observers.
It sustained vigorous missions, Bible institutes and evangelism when mainline zeal was declining.
It saw early that institutional drift could empty churches of their founding faith.
positions/fundamentalism/strongestObject: Critics argue that it made secondary matters (a particular inerrancy theory, premillennialism, young-earth creationism) into tests of faith.
Separatism produced endless splits, harsh polemics and anti-intellectualism, as later evangelicals such as Carl Henry (The Uneasy Conscience of Modern Fundamentalism, 1947) lamented.
Its "defence" of Scripture sometimes relied on modern rationalist assumptions (Baconian common-sense realism) rather than historic doctrine.
Its political turn (Moral Majority) is criticised for fusing faith with partisan politics.
positions/fundamentalism/responses/0: Fundamentalists reply that the essentials they defended were not novel but confessional, and that separation from denial of the gospel is commanded (2 Cor 6:17; 2 John 10).
positions/fundamentalism/responses/1: Many acknowledge excesses of militancy while insisting that the core doctrinal concerns were vindicated by the decline of liberal churches.
positions/fundamentalism/consequences/0: Lost control of the northern Presbyterian and Baptist denominations in the 1920s–30s, then built a parallel network of schools, radio and missions.
positions/fundamentalism/consequences/1: Gave rise, via reform from within, to the neo-evangelical movement of the 1940s.
positions/fundamentalism/consequences/2: Shaped American creationism debates and the Religious Right.
positions/fundamentalism/consequences/3: Exported to mission fields, influencing churches in Africa, Asia and Latin America.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/altNames/2: Theology of the Word of God
positions/neo-orthodoxy/oneLine: Against liberalism, God is "wholly other" and known only through his self-revelation in Jesus Christ, the one Word of God attested by Scripture and proclaimed by the Church, which judges all human religion and culture.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/coreClaims/0: God is known only by God’s free self-revelation, not by natural theology or religious experience.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/coreClaims/1: Jesus Christ is the one Word of God; Scripture is the witness to that Word and becomes God’s Word as God speaks through it.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/coreClaims/2: Human sin and the crisis of judgement are taken with radical seriousness; grace is God’s free act.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/coreClaims/3: The Church exists to hear and proclaim the Word, independent of state and culture.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/coreClaims/4: In Barth’s mature theology, election is God’s choice of all humanity in Christ.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/origin: Triggered by the support of Karl Barth’s liberal teachers for the German war effort (manifesto of 93 intellectuals, 1914). Barth’s Epistle to the Romans (1919; rewritten 1922), with Eduard Thurneysen, Friedrich Gogarten and Emil Brunner, launched "dialectical theology"; Barth’s Church Dogmatics (1932–67) developed it. In the US, Reinhold and H. Richard Niebuhr represented a related "Christian realism". Its political expression was the Barmen Declaration (1934).
positions/neo-orthodoxy/strongestArgumen: It recovered the transcendence and freedom of God and the centrality of Christ after liberalism’s collapse in 1914.
Its stress on the Word over culture enabled the Confessing Church’s resistance to Nazism.
It reconnected modern theology with the Reformers and the Fathers while accepting historical criticism.
Barth’s Church Dogmatics is widely regarded as the most important Protestant theology of the 20th century.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/strongestObjecti: Conservative evangelicals (Cornelius Van Til, The New Modernism, 1946; Carl Henry) objected that saying Scripture "becomes" the Word of God undermines its objective inspiration and inerrancy.
Liberals and existentialists (Bultmann, Tillich) found it fideist, cutting faith off from reason and culture; Brunner disputed its rejection of natural theology (Barth’s "Nein!", 1934).
Catholic and evangelical critics worry that Barth’s doctrine of election tends toward universalism.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/responses/0: Barthians reply that Scripture’s authority rests on God’s living speech through it, not on a theory of inerrancy, and that this is closer to the Reformers.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/responses/1: Barth insisted he did not teach universalism as a doctrine, leaving final outcomes to God’s freedom while hoping for all.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/consequences/0: Shaped mid-20th-century mainline Protestant theology, ecumenism (WCC) and seminaries worldwide.
positions/neo-orthodoxy/consequences/1: Grounded the Barmen Declaration and later confessions of resistance (e.g. Belhar, 1986).
positions/neo-orthodoxy/consequences/2: Barth’s influence revived from the 1990s among evangelicals and in Trinitarian theology (T. F. Torrance).
positions/evangelicalism/oneLine: A transdenominational Protestant movement marked by conversion, the authority of the Bible, the centrality of Christ’s cross and active evangelism and service, seeking to engage the world rather than withdraw from it.
positions/evangelicalism/coreClaims/0: Conversionism: lives need to be changed by personal faith in Christ.
positions/evangelicalism/coreClaims/1: Biblicism: the Bible is the supreme authority for faith and life.
positions/evangelicalism/coreClaims/2: Crucicentrism: Christ’s atoning death is the heart of the gospel.
positions/evangelicalism/coreClaims/3: Activism: the gospel must be expressed in evangelism, mission and service (Bebbington’s quadrilateral).
positions/evangelicalism/coreClaims/4: Cooperation across denominations on the basis of shared essentials.
positions/evangelicalism/origin: Rooted in the 18th-century revivals (Edwards, Whitefield, Wesley) and 19th-century missionary and reform movements. After the fundamentalist–modernist split, "new evangelicals" (Harold Ockenga, Carl F. H. Henry, Billy Graham) formed the National Association of Evangelicals (1942), Fuller Theological Seminary (1947) and Christianity Today (1956). The Lausanne Congress (1974) globalised it, with Latin American, African and Asian voices shaping "integral mission".
positions/evangelicalism/strongestArgume: It combines historic Protestant orthodoxy with energetic mission, producing one of the fastest-growing Christian movements worldwide.
Its transdenominational character allows cooperation in evangelism, relief and Bible translation.
Through Lausanne it integrated evangelism and social responsibility.
It engages scholarship and culture rather than retreating into separatism.
positions/evangelicalism/strongestObject: Fundamentalists criticise its cooperation with liberals and Catholics (e.g. Graham’s 1957 New York crusade).
Catholic, Orthodox and mainline critics argue it is individualistic, weak on ecclesiology and sacraments, and prone to consumerism and celebrity culture.
In the US its close association with partisan politics since the 1980s has, critics argue, compromised its witness; scandals of abuse and authoritarian leadership have damaged trust.
Scholars dispute whether "evangelical" names a coherent theological movement or a political-cultural identity.
positions/evangelicalism/responses/0: Evangelicals reply that cooperation in proclamation does not imply doctrinal compromise and that the gospel transcends denominations.
positions/evangelicalism/responses/1: Global evangelical leaders stress that most evangelicals now live in the Global South, where the political profile is different from the US.
positions/evangelicalism/consequences/0: Became one of the largest Christian movements: Pew (2011) estimated about 285 million evangelicals (about 13% of Christians) in 2010, with broader definitions giving higher figures.
positions/evangelicalism/consequences/1: Shaped global missions, Bible translation, relief agencies (World Vision, Tearfund) and media.
positions/evangelicalism/consequences/2: Became a major political force in the US, Brazil and elsewhere.
positions/ecumenism/oneLine: Divided churches should seek visible unity in faith, sacraments, ministry and mission, as Christ prayed "that they all may be one".
positions/ecumenism/coreClaims/0: Christian division contradicts Christ’s will and hinders mission (John 17:21).
positions/ecumenism/coreClaims/1: Churches should pray, study, work and witness together and pursue doctrinal agreement through dialogue.
positions/ecumenism/coreClaims/2: Mutual recognition of baptism is the basis of a real though imperfect communion.
positions/ecumenism/coreClaims/3: The goal (variously understood) is visible unity: organic union, reconciled diversity or full communion.
positions/ecumenism/origin: Grew from 19th-century missionary cooperation, student movements and the Evangelical Alliance (1846). The World Missionary Conference at Edinburgh (1910) led to the Life and Work (Stockholm 1925) and Faith and Order (Lausanne 1927) movements, which merged in the World Council of Churches (Amsterdam, 1948). Church unions followed (United Church of Canada 1925; Church of South India 1947; Church of North India 1970). The Catholic Church entered with Vatican II’s Unitatis Redintegratio (1964); key fruits include the lifting of the 1054 anathemas (1965), BEM (1982) and the Joint Declaration on Justification (1999).
positions/ecumenism/strongestArguments/0: Jesus prayed for his disciples’ unity "that the world may believe"; division is a scandal to mission.
positions/ecumenism/strongestArguments/1: Dialogue has resolved or softened historic disputes (e.g. justification 1999; Christological agreements with the Oriental Orthodox and the Assyrian Church of the East, 1994).
positions/ecumenism/strongestArguments/2: Shared witness has strengthened Christians’ response to persecution, injustice (apartheid) and poverty.
positions/ecumenism/strongestObjections/: Conservative evangelicals and fundamentalists argue that it subordinates truth to unity and includes churches that deny essential doctrines.
Some Orthodox (Georgia and Bulgaria left the WCC in 1997–98) and traditionalist Catholics see it as relativising the one true Church.
Critics charge the WCC with political partisanship (e.g. Programme to Combat Racism grants to liberation movements, 1970s).
Institutional ecumenism has stalled on ministry and Eucharist, and new divisions over sexuality have arisen.
positions/ecumenism/responses/0: Ecumenists reply that unity is sought "in truth" through rigorous theological dialogue, not minimalism.
positions/ecumenism/responses/1: They point to grassroots and "receptive" ecumenism and to forums such as the Global Christian Forum (2007), which include Pentecostals and evangelicals.
positions/ecumenism/consequences/0: Produced the WCC, national councils and many bilateral dialogues.
positions/ecumenism/consequences/1: Transformed Catholic–Protestant and Catholic–Orthodox relations from hostility to fraternity.
positions/ecumenism/consequences/2: Created united churches, notably in South Asia.
positions/ecumenism/consequences/3: Provoked separate evangelical and fundamentalist networks (e.g. International Council of Christian Churches, 1948).
